clinicalPearls: SLC35C1 encodes the Golgi GDP-fucose transporter; its deficiency impairs fucosylation of glycoproteins and glycolipids, giving both a type IIc congenital disorder of glycosylation and leukocyte adhesion deficiency type II.
Defective synthesis of the fucosylated selectin ligand sialyl-Lewis X abolishes leukocyte rolling along activated endothelium, so neutrophils cannot extravasate to sites of infection.
This produces recurrent bacterial infections that characteristically lack pus, together with a persistent, marked peripheral neutrophilic leukocytosis.
Absence of the fucosylated H antigen results in the rare Bombay blood-group phenotype.
Non-immune features are prominent and often dominate: severe growth restriction, microcephaly, marked intellectual disability and a distinctive facies.

Some patients improve clinically and biochemically with oral fucose supplementation, which drives the salvage pathway to restore selectin-ligand expression and reduce infections, though the response is mutation-dependent.

Unlike leukocyte adhesion deficiency type I, the defect lies in the rolling step of the adhesion cascade rather than in firm integrin-mediated adhesion, and delayed umbilical cord separation is not characteristic.
reference.pathophysiology: SLC35C1 is the nucleotide-sugar transporter that moves GDP-fucose from the cytosol into the Golgi lumen, where fucosyltransferases add fucose to glycans. Loss of function starves the Golgi of its fucose donor, so cells cannot synthesise fucosylated structures including sialyl-Lewis X, the ligand for E- and P-selectins, and the H and Lewis blood-group antigens. Without sialyl-Lewis X, leukocytes fail to tether and roll along activated endothelium, blocking the initial step of the leukocyte adhesion cascade and preventing recruitment to sites of infection despite a brisk marrow response, which explains the leukocytosis without pus. Widespread hypofucosylation of other glycoproteins underlies the growth failure and neurodevelopmental impairment. Because the fucose salvage pathway can regenerate GDP-fucose, exogenous fucose partially bypasses the defect in responsive individuals. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type I (ITGB2 / CD18 defect)
Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type III (FERMT3 / kindlin-3 defect)
Chronic granulomatous disease and other neutrophil-function defects
Congenital or cyclical neutropenia (here counts are conspicuously high rather than low)
Other congenital disorders of glycosylation with growth failure and developmental delay
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film showing persistent marked neutrophilic leukocytosis
Flow cytometry for sialyl-Lewis X (CD15s) on leukocytes
Blood group typing to detect the Bombay phenotype
Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing (a type II pattern in some patients)
Neutrophil adhesion and rolling functional studies in a specialist laboratory
Supervised trial of oral fucose with monitoring of counts and selectin-ligand expression
redFlags: Recurrent severe bacterial infection without abscess or pus formation
Persistent extreme leukocytosis mistaken for a leukaemoid reaction or malignancy
Aggressive periodontitis and non-healing soft-tissue infection
Failure to thrive with neurodevelopmental regression
reference.prognosis: Susceptibility to infection may attenuate somewhat with age and can improve on fucose supplementation in responsive individuals, but the neurodevelopmental disability and growth impairment are generally persistent.
pitfalls: Mistaking the persistent leukocytosis for a haematological malignancy or leukaemoid reaction
Overlooking the diagnosis because infections lack the expected purulent response
Failing to offer a supervised fucose trial in confirmed cases
Confusing the rolling defect of type II disease with the firm-adhesion CD18 defect of type I
references: Congenital disorders of glycosylation review literature
management: Give oral fucose supplementation to drive the salvage pathway, restore sialyl-Lewis X expression and reduce infections in responsive individuals
Treat bacterial infections promptly with appropriate antibiotics and consider antibiotic prophylaxis given the impaired neutrophil recruitment
Keep immunisations up to date and reinforce infection-prevention measures
Alert the blood bank to the Bombay phenotype to ensure compatible transfusion
Provide nutritional support for the growth restriction and developmental therapies for the intellectual disability and microcephaly
Monitor neutrophil counts, selectin-ligand expression and the biochemical response to fucose
Offer genetic counselling and family testing for autosomal recessive inheritance within multidisciplinary immunology and metabolic care
